sents.text: So far: one command, one job.
Today, commands start working together.
Wildcards let one command handle many files.
Redirection saves output to a file.
And pipes chain commands into a little assembly line.
This is where the terminal becomes a power tool.
A wildcard is a pattern that matches file names.
The star matches any run of characters, so star dot csv means every file ending in dot csv.
The question mark matches exactly one character.
And square brackets match one character from a set, like day one, two or three.
The shell expands the pattern before the command even runs, so any command can use it.
ls star dot csv lists them; cp star dot csv data slash copies them all at once.
And rm with a wildcard deletes them all at once, so always run ls with the same pattern first, to see exactly what will go.
Every command has three streams.
Standard input, where it reads from.
Standard output, where its normal results go.
And standard error, where error messages go.
Normally, both outputs land on your screen.
Redirection and pipes let you send them somewhere else.
The greater-than sign sends output into a file instead of the screen.
Careful: a single greater-than replaces whatever was in the file.
Two of them, greater-than greater-than, add to the end instead.
The number two followed by greater-than sends just the error messages.
And less-than feeds a file in as input.
